title: How To Handle Sleepy, Unprepared, And Unmotivated Students otivated-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin acknowledges that students often arrive at school mentally and physically unready for learning, and argues teachers must proactively counteract this rather than leave it to chance. He describes a morning routine strategy: meeting students outside before the bell, setting a simple expectation (like a quiet, straight line) upon entry, moving them immediately into responsibilities like unpacking and organizing materials, and finishing with a tidy, pride-inducing routine before the first announcement. If students still seem sluggish, he suggests brief physical activity like jumping jacks to boost alertness. The piece frames this brisk, purposeful morning sequence as 'flipping a switch' that associates the school bell with focus and energy rather than drowsiness.
points: Students often arrive physically and mentally unready to learn; teachers must proactively counteract this rather than leaving it to chance.
Meet students outside the classroom before the bell rather than letting them 'sleepwalk' directly into the room.
Set a simple expectation immediately after the bell (e.g., a quiet, straight line with backpacks zipped) to signal that school is now in session.
Move students immediately into purposeful morning responsibilities—unpacking, organizing materials, checking mailboxes—that have been previously taught and practiced.
If students remain sluggish, brief physical activity like jumping jacks can boost alertness, since exercise and mental performance are closely linked.
quotes: They enter your classroom bleary eyed. Some have bed-head and pillow lines etched on their faces.
The truth is, regardless of how strongly you harp on coming to school prepared, you can’t always count on students to arrive with the mental and physical sharpness needed for optimal learning.
The key to this strategy is not giving your students the opportunity to sleepwalk into your classroom.
Make sure your students have immediate and multiple responsibilities upon entering your classroom—prepping homework, hanging backpacks, organizing materials, checking mailboxes.
The relationship between exercise and mental performance is a close one; it pays to use it to your advantage.
By starting the day task focused and brisk moving, you’re grooving an association of attentiveness, independence, and responsibility with the ringing of the morning bell.
